newsitem.title: UK: Coffee producers meet as unrest mounts in Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Coffee producers meet as unrest mounts in Colombia.

text.p: The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) meets on Friday to review export figures and commitments against a background of mounting guerrilla unrest in group lynchpin, Colombia.
"Colombia's internal problems have reached a stage which is critical and coffee, a key export, is likely to come under further pressure," said one London-based analyst.

But traders and ACPC delegates said a wave of leftist guerrilla attacks and highway blockades across the country was unlikely to derail Colombia's commitment to ACPC efforts to stabilise supply and put a floor under coffee prices.
Colombia is the world's second-largest producer after Brazil with exports representing about 18 percent of total world supply.
Colombia's coffee exporters have already felt the effects of the rebel violence, announcing this week that some coffee shipments would have to be delayed.
"The guerrillas are definitely seeking to upset the apple cart," added the analyst.

Offensives over the past few months by Colombia's largest rebel forces, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the National Liberation Army (ELN), have split the country and brought chaos to overland transport.

"There are grave concerns about guerrillas because they're not bothered what grade of coffee we're hauling, they just set it on fire. It's a strategy designed to sow panic," said a Colombian private exporter.
Some coffee traders this week hinted domestic problems might deflect Colombia's attention at the two day meeting of ACPC, that represents 80 percent of world production.
But ACPC sources saw this as unrealistic.
"The Federation (Colombia's coffee federation) is fully committed to the ACPC. I would ignore any talk of flailing commitment," said a source, familiar with Colombian policy.
At its meeting on Friday and Saturday, the ACPC will contemplate the effectiveness of its 1995/96 and 1996/97 export plans and review the market situation.
The ACPC last met in May when it agreed a new plan to limit green coffee exports from its 14 members to 53.5 million 60-kg bags in the year to June 1997 against 45.8 million in 1995/96.
ACPC Secretary-General Roberio Oliviera Silva said preliminary figures showed ACPC exports in the 1995/96 period reached 47 million 60-kilo bags against the target of 45.8 million.
"I am very happy with that figure. It shows we are able to coordinate our efforts in terms of putting a floor under supply," Oliviera told Reuters.
Since the ACPC's last meeting in May, second-month robusta coffee futures have slid from $1,970 a tonne to their lowest level in over two years at $1,475 a tonne.

When asked if the ACPC was concerned about recent price falls, Oliviera said: "We are always concerned about the price evolution, especially when prices fall. We will analyse the market situation. It is on the agenda."
